title: The library that was lost
hook: the Sikh Reference Library, with old handwritten manuscripts, was lost in the operation's aftermath

segments.voice: Yesterday, June 1984: the army in the Harmandir complex on a holy day, the Akal Takht damaged, and your line, remember the pilgrims. Today, a quieter loss from the same days, one made of paper and ink. Day three hundred nine.

Think of the oldest thing your family owns. A letter from a great-grandparent. A wedding photograph gone brown at the edges. A recipe written in a hand nobody alive can match. If a fire took it, you could never buy it back. There's no shop for that. Now imagine a whole building of those things, but for an entire people: the handwriting of their history, some of it centuries old. That building stood inside the Harmandir complex until June 1984. Today: the library that was lost.
screen: `THE OLDEST THING YOUR FAMILY OWNS.` → `NO SHOP SELLS IT BACK.` → `A WHOLE BUILDING OF THEM.`

segments.voice: It was called the Sikh Reference Library, set up in the complex in the 1940s. What was in it? Handwritten copies of the Guru Granth Sahib, some very old, copied out by hand long before printing. Hukamnamas: letters and orders sent by the Gurus themselves to Sikh communities, some in the Gurus' own time. Rare books, old histories, documents of the Singh Sabha and the gurdwara reform movement. Scholars came from far away to read there. It was the memory of the community on shelves. In the days after the fighting in June 1984, the library burned. How it happened is disputed. The army's account says it caught fire during the fighting. Many Sikhs, and some witnesses, say the fighting had ended first, and that the building was burned afterward, and that boxes of material were carried away before the fire. Over the years, some items have been returned. Many have never been found. Sikh bodies still ask for the rest to be given back, and the question is still open. Why does a library matter so much, in a week when people died? Because Sikhs are a people of a book. The Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru, and handwritten copies carried the Guru's word across generations. A hukamnama in a Guru's hand is a thread straight back to them. Losing them is like losing the family letters, except the family is a whole community. It's a loss you only feel fully when you understand what memory is: not just knowledge, but connection.
screen: `THE SIKH REFERENCE LIBRARY.` · `HANDWRITTEN GRANTHS AND HUKAMNAMAS.` · `IT BURNED; HOW IS DISPUTED.` · `A PEOPLE OF A BOOK.` · then, large: `MEMORY IS PRECIOUS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold something old. If you can, find an old book, a photograph, a letter, anything that carries someone's memory. Hold it in your hands. Look at it slowly: the paper, the handwriting, the wear at the corners. If there's nothing old nearby, picture one. Think of who made it, and who kept it safe so it could reach you. Let yourself be grateful to the keepers. Then rest with the breath, holding it gently. The bell holds the time.
The library that was lost. The Sikh Reference Library, with handwritten Granths and the Gurus' letters, burned in the days after the June 1984 operation.
screen: `THE LIBRARY THAT WAS LOST — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: memory is precious. Today, save one family memory somewhere safe: scan a photo, write down a story, or ask someone older to tell it. Day three hundred nine.

howItsDone: Sikh institutions continue to ask for the return of manuscripts and documents from the Sikh Reference Library, and Sikhs remember its loss as part of the June remembrance each year.

original.note: Gurmukhi: hukamnama, a letter of command; the Gurus sent them to Sikh communities.

trapdoor: what you thought: a library is a room of books.
what it means: the community's memory on shelves: handwritten Granths and the Gurus' own letters.
what a scholar hears: the Sikh Reference Library, founded in 1946, burned on June 6 or 7, 1984; the SGPC's claims for the return of seized material remain unresolved.
